definition: a written, bounded, consequence-anchored commitment to what a system is engineered to withstand. It names the consequences that must not happen and the bounded set of conditions the system is built to survive, and it serves as the yardstick every adequacy argument is measured against. Borrowed from nuclear safety engineering.
the specific, concrete outcome that must not happen, stated in the system's own terms, from which the whole design basis is derived. The fixed point everything else traces back to.

the explicitly stated set of adversary capabilities and conditions a design is engineered to defeat — and, just as explicitly, what falls outside it. Bounding the adversary (rather than chasing every threat) is what makes the discipline tractable and testable.

*Design Basis Accident* is the classic nuclear instantiation: postulated accidents (equipment failure, natural hazard) the plant's safety systems must bring to a safe state. *Design Basis Accident — Military Action* is this work's extension of the same method to deliberate adversary action, including cyber and kinetic/military threats.
the design basis for the facility or facility class; anchors on physical/operational must-not-happens, bounds a physical/kinetic/operational adversary.

the design basis for the AI operating in or over the facility; *inherits* the FC-DB's consequence root (and may extend it), but bounds a distinct adversary envelope — model manipulation, data poisoning, prompt injection, autonomy drift. The reason the AI is not covered by the facility's DB.
the relationship between the two design bases: shared consequence root, different adversary envelope. The keystone result of the course.

they differ in epistemology, not rigor. Risk management works against a threat envelope it never formally bounds; a design basis formally bounds the envelope and carries a forcing function that triggers review when a threat exceeds it. Without that function, risk assumptions drift silently.

the boundary, defined in the AI-DB, past which the AI's action could reach the facility's must-not-happen consequences; the seam where the AI design basis fastens to the facility's. Must be *bright* — observably crossed or not. (Written as two words, no hyphen, in the governance sense — the consequence-reachability seam.) Defined in FD-BL (*The Bright Line*) as a threshold on actions: each action is placed above or below the line on its own consequence.

the AI-DB's severity scale: how much the AI's failure matters, measured against the inherited consequences. Structured as the SIL-equivalent (functional-safety Safety Integrity Level analog) for AI; a higher band means greater reach to worse consequences and correspondingly greater assurance obligations. Three bands — **Highest, Mid, Lowest** — set by the worst reachable consequence (take-the-max). Orthogonal to the **error class**, which names *what kind* of cognitive error is assessed. (Retired numeric labels: Tier 1/2/3.)

the kind of cognitive error an assessment targets: *safety-critical*, *quality-of-service*, or *compliance*. Orthogonal to the criticality band — the band says how much is at stake, the error class says which kind of failure the assessment is hunting. The Tiered Assessment Framework assesses across all three.

The Broker for industrial and control settings: the qualified human who gives the substantive, attributable authorization the Bright Line requires before an above-line action executes. Defined as a role, not a component, in FD-BR (*The Broker*), which pairs it to FD-BL (*The Bright Line*). It works with the **Gate**, the enforcement interlock that makes an above-line action impossible to execute without authorization; the Gate never authorizes and never stands in for the Broker. The course's result is that the Command Broker is also the **arbiter of design basis collisions**: where both the FC-DB and the AI-DB have a legitimate claim on the same decision, the Broker settles it at decision speed, since neither basis outranks the other. Distinct from the CDB- communications design basis.

The role-type, defined in FD-BR (*The Broker*), that discharges a Bright Line's authorization obligation: a qualified human, not an office, a software component, or a procedure telling someone to confirm. Each Broker is paired to one Line, and the role does not transfer between Lines. There are two instantiations: the **Command Broker**, paired to FD-BL (*The Bright Line*), and the **Influence Broker**, paired to the surveillance Bright Line. With the Line and the Gate, the Broker completes the enforcement triad: the Line places the obligation, the Gate enforces it, and the Broker authorizes.

the relationship between the two design bases. They are not a hierarchy: the AI-DB inherits the FC-DB's *consequences*, not its *authority*. The merge is discharged by making the seam itself the governed object — an assignable duty to detect conflict before acting, with a fallback when conflict cannot be removed. Modeled on the nuclear safety/security interface (10 CFR 73.58).

the course's supporting-reference unit: a source excerpt placed in context under the heading it serves, with what it establishes and where the AI case departs from it. Numbered by module (M03-CN-01) and collected in `resources/course-notes/`. Not a reading list.

The runtime architecture that makes advance discharge possible under *Mode of Discharge* (FD-BL-D1): an unverifiable *proposer* (the AI) holds proposal authority only, while a simple, deterministic, formally verified *gatekeeper* holds veto authority and is the sole path to the process. The safety case lives entirely in the gatekeeper. The gatekeeper is not a second kind of broker: the Command Broker authorizes the envelope the gatekeeper enforces.

The determination under FD-BL (*The Bright Line*) of whether the Command Broker's authorization may, for a narrow class of above-line actions, be discharged *in advance* rather than in the moment. It may, if and only if three conditions all hold. R1: the whole safety case lives in a formally verified gatekeeper that the proposing AI can neither modify nor bypass. R2: the gatekeeper's acceptance set is proven safe over state, trajectory and rate, so that *which* action is chosen, and not merely *whether* it is allowed, is bounded. R3: changes *to* the pre-authorized envelope are excluded. The human authorization is not skipped but relocated in time: a qualified human authorized the envelope and accepted the proof. Where the proof fails, the action takes in-the-moment authorization. Formerly listed here as *Advance discharge*.

the determination that an authorization is bounded only if the state it is granted against is real. Generative output that can ground an above-line authorization must be traceable to independently verifiable values (I2) and must not be the sole basis for it (I3); a broker or gatekeeper acting on a corrupted or drifted picture is *confident and wrong*.

the terminology reservation. **"Envelope"** is reserved for the *authorization* object (the region within which an above-line action is pre-authorized; changing it is an R3 event); the *monitoring* object — a region of normal operation whose violation is a runtime event to detect — is the **operating band**. Distinct from the *adversary envelope* of the design-basis method (the bounded threat set), which is a different concept.

The governing layer the whole corpus conforms to, held as one dated edition, currently the **October 2026 Edition**. Each idea is defined once, and every other document cites it by name and section rather than restating it; where wording differs, the definition governs. The five definitions are FD-BL (*The Bright Line*), FD-LD (*Layer Decomposition and Determinism*), FD-EV (*The Envelope*), FD-BR (*The Broker*) and FD-LS (*Local Sovereignty*). Two determinations sit under the Bright Line and settle questions it left open: FD-BL-D1 (*Mode of Discharge*) and FD-BL-D2 (*Indication Integrity*). They are not definitions. The course's primitives are the teaching form of these instruments.

The companion to the Foundational Definitions, not a member of the family. It holds the current version of every definition, so a citation names the section, not the version, and resolves to the current text here. A citation that pinned a version would lead a reader to superseded text once the definition was revised.
a carved category of facilities alike enough in consequence and adversary profile that a single design basis can serve the whole category. Justified by the strategic-significance boundary.
the line a category of facility crosses when its systematic loss would reach a national or systemic consequence, justifying elevation to a standing facility class.

the test for whether the (military-action) design basis applies to a specific facility: geolocation relative to defense-critical loads, position in strategic transport corridors, substitutability, and adversary targeting logic. Disjunctive for a positive determination (any one filter puts a facility in scope); cumulative and documented for a negative one; built to fail toward inclusion. (Author's Section 1.4 / OI-8 gate, canonicalized in DBA-MA-AF.)

the procedure that proportions assessment depth to criticality, assessing the cognitive-layer errors of generative AI. Uses two orthogonal scales: criticality band (Highest/Mid/Lowest) and error class (safety-critical / quality-of-service / compliance).

A property of a protective function, defined in FD-LS (*Local Sovereignty*): the function executes on physical law, is colocated with the asset it protects, and requires no authority from any reachable system to act. It is a property of a function, not of a device, and all three conditions must hold. The burden of proof is on the intermediation, not on the independence. Embodied by the Aurora Disruptor.

a passive, analog protective device that blocks Aurora-style attacks on rotating machinery using only physical inputs (grid frequency and its rate of change); the canonical hardware embodiment of Local Sovereignty and the Bright Line. Deployed at scale in Operation Rockridge.

generative *produces* outputs; agentic *acts* toward a goal across steps; autonomous acts *without a human in the loop*. The governance-relevant boundary is where an autonomous system crosses into safety-critical reach.

an AI system (or coordinated network) that detects, amplifies, and directs influence at scale with enough autonomy that no human authorizes its specific outputs; operates via an aggregate→profile→generate→deliver pipeline. The policy branch's canonical threat.

the governance remedy to the AIB: a mandatory human authorization point interposed between the generation and delivery stages, architecturally non-bypassable, which also restores accountability. The information-domain analog of the Command Broker. Under FD-BR (*The Broker*) it is the Broker paired to the surveillance Bright Line, and it is not a Command Broker.
the point at which an AI's synthesis of individually innocuous, legally obtained data crosses into functional mass surveillance; the trigger condition for an Influence Broker mandate.

*punishment* (attack will be attributed and punished), *denial* (attack will not succeed against a hardened target), and *resilience* (system recovers faster than the campaign can sustain). Denial is the form design-basis standards most directly produce.

Able to keep performing a critical function, without degradation, under the hazards and loads in its design basis. Robustness is measured as *margin*. It is a design-basis property: past the design basis, a robust system may fail abruptly. Robustness is the engineering property that deterrence by denial rests on. Contrast **Resilient**.

Able to hold a defined minimum level of a critical function while degraded, and to restore full function within a defined time. Resilience is measured *over time*: how far function drops, for how long, and how fast it recovers. It governs events beyond the design basis, or events the design basis did not anticipate, and it is the engineering property behind deterrence by resilience. Contrast **Robust**.

Having more than one means of performing a function. Redundancy protects against random, independent failures but not against a common cause: identical channels share the same weaknesses, including the same cyber exploit. Redundancy is not robustness unless the redundant means are also **Diverse** and **Independent**.

Performing the same function by means that differ in principle, technology, supplier or dependency, so that no single cause can defeat them all. Diversity is the defense against *common-cause failure*. Examples: a digital controller backed by a hard-wired interlock; chlorination with an independent backup feed; fiber backed by licensed radio.

Free of shared dependencies (power, communications, software, location, staff or vendor), so that the failure of one means cannot cause the failure of another. Without independence, diversity exists on paper but not in practice. The course's *independent barriers* and *independent backstops* use the word in this sense.

A design principle from nuclear safety that applies across all critical infrastructure sectors. Each critical function is protected by means strong enough to withstand its design basis, and different and independent enough that no single physical, cyber or supply-chain cause defeats them all. It is the design-basis foundation that resilience builds on: Robust and Diverse limits how often and how badly a function degrades; resilience governs what happens when it degrades anyway.

the course's premise: no critical-infrastructure sector but nuclear was ever required to define a formal design basis, leaving most of critical-infrastructure protection without the discipline that makes safety engineering rigorous — a gap that turns acute once autonomous AI enters these systems.

*Consequence-driven Cyber-informed Engineering* (the acute, consequence-first methodology formalized at Idaho National Laboratory) and *Cyber-Informed Engineering* (the broader design philosophy of building cyber-consequence reasoning into engineering from the start). The lineage this course's method stands on.
